text: Differentiating common swine respiratory conditions: Mycoplasma (the most common cause of coughing in Cambodia) damages the respiratory tract, opening the door to secondary Pasteurella and severe pneumonia; a day/night temperature swing over 10°C in the building favors it. Signs: 7–8 coughs per episode, strongest in early morning, moderate fever (~39.5°C), reduced but not absent appetite; typically starts around 2 months of age (though contamination happens right after weaning), improves with treatment but tends to recur until slaughter. Treatment: Oxytetracycline, Doxycycline, Tylosin, or Florfenicol — not Amoxicillin, which is ineffective against Mycoplasma (it may look like it's working since it kills secondary Pasteurella, but coughing returns, often worse, a few days after stopping). Prevention: mix Doxycycline or Florfenicol into feed for 10–15 days right after weaning (when maternal antibody protection ends), and again for 5–7 days when moving pigs from post-weaning to fattening pens (a stressful transition that can trigger Mycoplasma). Swine Flu (viral, H1N1-type — not yet identified in Cambodia as of the source's writing): very acute — healthy one day, 90% of pigs sick the next, with severe coughing, labored breathing, and fever above 40°C; recovery in about 5 days; no treatment (viral), but antibiotics (e.g. Oxytetracycline for 3–5 days) help prevent secondary bacterial infection. Pasteurellosis (often combined with Mycoplasma): pus nasal discharge, short but painful coughing, rapid breathing, fever over 40°C, and blue-discolored skin especially at the ear tips (distinct from PRRS); treat severe cases with Tetracycline, Florfenicol, or Enrofloxacin (double dose on day 1, but be aware regular Enrofloxacin use breeds resistance); the best prevention is good Mycoplasma control, since Pasteurella normally lives harmlessly in the respiratory tract and only becomes a problem when pigs are already weakened — vaccinating against Pasteurella itself is not useful. Actinobacillus (bacterial): very acute, 12-hour incubation — bloody froth from the nose, short cough (1–3 at a time), severe breathing difficulty, fever over 40°C, severe depression, and death; treat with Amoxicillin, TMP+Sulfa, or Enrofloxacin. Lung lesions differ by disease and are worth checking at necropsy for Pasteurellosis and Actinobacillus (which do cause death); Mycoplasma lesions are typically only seen at slaughter, since pigs rarely die directly from it.
